title: On-chip photonic crystal dressed Rydberg exciton polaritons with enhanced nonlinearity in monolayer WS_2

paper_content.abstract: Rydberg exciton polaritons are promising for quantum optoelectronic devices exploiting their strong optical nonlinearities. Conventional polaritonic devices consist of optical microcavities made by vertically stacking distributed Bragg reflectors (DBR) and/or metallic mirrors and excitonic active regions, which may restrain their applicability in photonic integrated technologies. Here, we demonstrate the first on-chip photonic crystal (PhC) Rydberg polaritons based on monolayer WS2, which survive up to 80 K. These Rydberg polaritons exhibit a nonlinearity 8.0 ± 2.3 times larger than that of the ground polaritonic states due mostly to their extended exciton radii and, additionally, due to a stronger spatially localized electric field distribution compared to the dual-DBR geometry. Furthermore, the coexistence of 2s and 1s polaritonic states enables us to experimentally quantify their cross-interaction constant (14.4 ± 6.8 μeV μm2). The first realization of on-chip Rydberg polaritons represents a solid step towards polaritonic-based integrated circuits.
paper_content.introduction:
Exciton polaritons, hybrid light−matter bosonic particles induced by the strong coupling of photons and excitons, can exhibit long spatial and temporal coherences, small effective masses derived from their photonic constituent, and strong nonlinearities and long lifetimes inherited from the excitonic constituent1,2. Such hybrid quasi-particles have emerged as ideal candidates for implementing and manipulating many-body physics phenomena such as Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC)1–3, solitons4,5, and quantized vortices6,7, which can be harnessed in ultrafast polaritonic transistors and switches8,9, polaritonic interferometers10, and topological polaritonic architectures11,12. Recently, analog polariton simulators of complex Hamiltonians have been implemented by exploiting the interaction between neighbouring polariton condensates13.

To push these technologies into the quantum regime14, one option consists of enhancing polariton-polariton interactions and attaining the polariton-blockade regime15, in which the interaction strength between two polaritons is large enough to produce a shift of the polariton resonance larger than the polariton linewidth, thereby ensuring the generation of single-polariton states. Polaritonic nonlinear interactions, governed by the exciton oscillator strength, the exciton Bohr radius (aB), and the excitonic fraction of the polaritons employed15–17, are thus crucial for realizing polaritonic quantum technologies. In this context, Rydberg excitons, corresponding to excitonic excited states, constitute a promising approach to enhancing polaritonic nonlinearities. Rydberg exciton polaritons have been investigated in vertical Fabry-Perot cavities formed by distributed Bragg reflectors (DBR) and/or metal mirrors surrounding GaAs18,19, Cu2O20, WSe2 17, ReS2 21, and CsPbBr3 22 active regions, among which the TMD based Rydberg polaritons show a record nonlinearity (Table S1). Furthermore, because of their larger spatial extension, Rydberg excitons can also be regarded as a new means of enhanced optical sensing due to their larger sensitivity to their environment23,24, highlighting potential new applications of Rydberg exciton polaritons.

While vertical microcavities have enabled fundamental polaritonic studies, on-chip photonic structures ease their cascadability and improve the compactness of polaritonic devices25. With this aim, polaritons have been lately generated thanks to the coupling of excitonic resonances and photonic modes confined either in dielectric waveguides26–29 or in one- (1D) and two-dimensional (2D) photonic crystals (PhC) and metasurfaces30–34. Among the wide choice of polaritonic materials35 compatible with on-chip photonic structures, monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) appear as the most natural choice: on the one hand, they display excitons exhibiting very large oscillator strength36, and on the other hand, they can be easily exfoliated and transferred onto any material platform37. Indeed, TMD-based exciton polaritons have contributed in the last years to showcase fundamental polaritonic physics38,39, including BEC40, strong nonlinearities39, and parametric scattering41, as well as to implement optoelectronic devices exploiting the spin properties of TMD-based polaritons42. Different excitonic species, including dipolar exciton polaritons43, trion polaritons44, charged biexciton polaritons45, and Moiré polaritons46, have been widely demonstrated. Exciton-polaritons based on Moiré MoSe2/WS2 excitons46 and hybridized interlayer excitons in MoS2 bilayers43,47, have been reported to display the largest polariton nonlinearities, in the order of tens of μeV μm2.

In this work, we aim to demonstrate the first realization of on-chip Rydberg polaritons, employing WS2 monolayers on a 1D PhC cavity structure. PhCs enable engineering of the photonic constituent of the polaritons and, therefore, the polariton dispersion. By modifying the properties of the polaritons’ excitonic constituents through temperature and magnetic field, we observed 2s exciton polaritons up to 80 K with an increase of their Rabi energy by more than 14% at ± 9 T. Furthermore, the polariton-polariton nonlinearity of 2s Rydberg polaritons in the PhC is 8.0 ± 2.3 times larger than the polariton-polariton nonlinearity of polaritonic ground states. This enhancement arises mostly due to the larger exciton radius of 2s excitons. Additionally, PhC-induced confinement of polaritons in real space enables a 15-20% enhancement of nonlinearity compared with dual-DBR geometry. Furthermore, the simultaneous quenching of the oscillator strength (accounted for by the Fano q parameter) and broadening of the Fano resonances’ linewidth indicates the onset of the nonlinearity. These results provide an alternative strategy for enhanced nonlinearity of polariton species in TMD systems and pave the way for implementing integrated polaritonic quantum technologies.
paper_content.results:
Photonic crystal dressed 1s and 2s exciton polaritons
The system studied in this work is illustrated in Fig. 1a, where one monolayer WS2 and a thin hBN (~15 nm) flake are dry transferred onto a silicon nitride (SiN) based 1D PhC. The PhC is etched onto a 220 nm thick SiN layer, itself deposited onto a 1.2 μm thick SiO2 layer lying on a Si wafer. The 1D SiN PhC is fabricated via electron-beam lithography and reactive ion etching (Methods). Such 1D PhC exhibits anisotropic photonic dispersions that will, in turn, give rise to anisotropic polaritonic ones. Herein, we define X-polarization as the polarization in which the electric field is parallel to the PhC grooves (x-axis in Fig. 1a), and Y-polarization as the polarization in which the electric field is perpendicular to the grooves (y-axis in Fig. 1a). Figure 1b presents the experimental and simulated angle-resolved reflectance of X-polarized modes of the PhC structure with hBN but without monolayer WS2 on top. They exhibit two highly-dispersive modes (labeled as modes 1 and 2) around the targeted wavevectors and energies. Note that the mode dispersions are modulated by Fabry-Perot modes corresponding to the underlying thick SiO2 layer, as attested by the broad reflectance features from 2.10 to about 2.14 eV. These lossy Fabry-Perot modes display a negligible electric field intensity at the WS2 location and, therefore, barely modify the photoluminescence (PL) of the excitons and polaritons (Fig. S1). The electric field profiles in the y−z plane for the X-polarized mode 1 at the targeted angles and energies (red circles in Fig. 1b), corresponding to 1s and 2s energies at 4 K, are shown in Fig. 1c. The electric field intensity at the position where monolayer WS2 will be located (black dashed lines inside panels) is 0.6 and 0.8 times that of the maximum electric field intensity across the entire photonic structure for 1s and 2s excitons, respectively.

We first present the strong coupling in a hybrid hBN/WS2/PhC structure (device 1) at room temperature (RT), as shown in Fig. 2a. The two X-polarized modes 1 and 2 exhibit an anti-crossing around the ground excitonic state of WS2 (~2.01 eV), while the Y-polarized mode remains in the weak coupling regime due to a reduced overlap between the photonic mode and the exciton wavefunction (Fig. S2). The right panel in Fig. 2a shows the corresponding numerical simulation (Methods). Figure 2b shows the detailed angle-dependent reflection spectra at RT around the 1s exciton energy extracted from Fig. 2a. The spectra are fitted with two Lorentzian functions (solid curves in Fig. 2b) to obtain the upper polariton branch (UP) and the lower polariton branch (LP) peak positions, shown as dots in Fig. 2c (Methods). The obtained peak positions are further fitted with a coupled-oscillator model (solid curves in Fig. 2c) with a Rabi splitting in reflectivity (ΩRef) of 25.0 ± 2.0 meV. The corresponding exciton (X) and photon fractions (C) of UP and LP obtained are shown in Fig. 2d. In comparison, the damping rates for bare excitons and cavity photons are γexc = 22.8 meV and γcav = 19.0 meV, respectively (Fig. S3). Therefore, ΩRef is slightly larger than (γexc + γcav)/2 = 20.9 meV, confirming that the system operates in the strong coupling regime. Note that, taking into account the measured damping rates for excitons and photon modes, the actual Rabi splitting between the polariton resonances, defined by the energy separation between UP and LP, is indeed larger than the splitting observed in reflectivity, further confirming the achievement of strong coupling at RT48. Notably, given that within the same flake the bare exciton energy and γexc of WS2 can fluctuate depending on the actual environment (Fig. S4), the excitonic values used for the corresponding modelling of the polaritonic dispersions are those measured at the same location but at larger angles, typically ~30 degrees, where the exciton is not coupled to any photonic mode. Alternatively, such bare exciton properties could also be obtained from measurements in Y-polarization, for which the system operates in the weak coupling regime (Fig. S5)31.

Upon cooling down the sample to 4 K and performing angle-resolved reflectance in device 1, as shown in Fig. 2e, a second anti-crossing around the energy of 2s exciton state of WS2 appears, confirming the coupling of the 2s excitons to the PhC optical mode. In addition, the X-polarized mode 1 also couples to the 1s exciton state with an energy separation of 35.0 ± 3.0 meV, larger than that at RT due to the narrowing of the excitonic line. The corresponding PL emission further confirms the occurrence of strong coupling for 1s exciton polaritons (Fig. S1). Figure 2f plots the detailed angle-dependent reflection spectra around the 2s Rydberg exciton in Fig. 2e. The spectra are fitted with two Lorentzian functions (solid curves in Fig. 2f) to obtain UP and LP peak positions (Methods), shown as dots in Fig. 2g. The obtained peak positions are further fitted with a coupled-oscillator model (solid curves in Fig. 2g) with a Rabi splitting in reflectivity (ΩRef) of 16.7 ± 1.5 meV. The corresponding X and C of UP and LP obtained for 1s and 2s polaritons at 4 K are shown in Fig. 2h. The damping rate for bare 2s excitons and cavity photons are γexc = 6.5 meV and γcav = 19.0 meV, respectively (Fig. S3). Again, ΩRef is larger than (γexc + γcav)/2 = 12.7 meV, reflecting that a narrower excitonic linewidth of 2s exciton makes it easier to fulfill the criterion for a given cavity photon linewidth (γcav) compared with 1s exciton.

The Rabi splitting we measure for the coupling between the 2s exciton and the PhC mode is twice the value of the Rabi splitting measured for the 2s exciton coupling to a cavity mode in a vertical microcavity (ref. 17), where three layers of monolayer TMD were stacked to overcome the reduced oscillator strength. The increased Rabi splitting in our structure is explained by the enhanced overlap between the exciton and the electric field of the PhC mode, which is confined to a subwavelength thickness, as opposed to the vertical DBR structure, where the photonic mode extends over several wavelengths (Figs. S6, S7, Supplementary Note 1). Notably, by positioning the active layers close to the maximum of the electric field, our obtained ΩRef for both 1s and 2s polaritons are comparable with that measured in planar DBR-based microcavities, in which the monolayer is located close to an antinode of the electric field distribution (Table S2). As the Rabi splitting is proportional to the square-root of the oscillator strength and the overlap between the active material and the photonic field (Supplementary Note 1)1, a Rabi splitting ratio between 1s and 2s polaritons of 2.2 could be calculated, which matches well our experimental results, i.e., 35/16.7 = 2.1.

Numerical simulations of the corresponding dispersions (right panel in Fig. 1e), show a clear anti-crossing feature for 1s and 2s excitons coupled with the X-polarized mode 1. To make sure our designed structure exhibits prominent coupling with 1s and 2s excitons, we optimized the polaritonic dispersion by varying three geometric parameters of the PhC, i.e., thickness of the grating (h), period of the unit cell (p), and the filling factor (FF, width of the unetched grating portion over the unit cell dimension) utilizing FDTD (“Methods”, Figs. S8–10). Note that the as-designed 1D PhC cannot only support guided mode resonances but also a so-called bound state in the continuum (BIC) mode at a wavevector equal to zero (Fig. S11)3, although in our study it does not couple to either of the excitonic resonances. However, the photonic branches leading to the BIC mode indeed do couple, exhibiting a coupling strength Ω of 38 ± 3 meV with the 1s excitons at 4 K and at a non zero wavevector.

Temperature and magnetic field dependent behaviors of 2s exciton polaritons
To assess the robustness of the strong coupling regime of 2s excitons in device 1, we conduct temperature and magnetic field-dependent angle-resolved reflectance measurements. The temperature-dependent reflectivity spectra (Figs. 3a, S12) indicate that Rydberg 2s exciton polaritons survive up to 80 K: indeed, the Rabi splitting is larger than (γexc + γcav)/2 at each temperature and ensures that the system operates in the strong coupling regime (Figs. S13–15 and Supplementary Note 2). Further increasing the temperature will enhance phonon scattering and accelerate exciton dephasing, consequently reducing the Rabi splitting31. Besides, temperature-dependent angle-resolved reflectance spectra around 1s excitons from 15 K to 295 K (Figs. S16–18) were also explored. The Rabi splitting is roughly constant (32–35 meV) from low temperatures up to about 200 K, consistent with an almost constant excitonic broadening (7−9 meV). As temperature increases further, the Rabi splitting decreases from 35 ± 3 to 25 ± 2 meV, while the linewidth of the 1s exciton increases from 9 to 25 meV, due to enhanced electron-phonon coupling and an acceleration of the exciton dephasing49. The Rabi splitting is thus also larger than (γexc + γcav)/2 at each temperature, ensuring the robustness of the strong coupling. Herein, the larger intrinsic exciton dephasing of 2s excitons compared to 1s excitons is mainly due to their smaller exciton binding energy and larger Bohr radius (Eb(2) is 1/9 of Eb(1))50, indicating a higher sensitivity of the 2s excitons to the surrounding environment, in particular to phonons50.

Note that we have used Fano resonances31 to fit the polariton dispersions, but whenever the q value was lower than 0.1, we used instead two Lorentzian functions to simplify, as the Fano resonance reproduces a Lorentzian when q = 0. Overall, in the current work we employed Fano resonances to fit the temperature dependence of 2s and 1s bare excitons (Figs. S14, S17) as well as to fit 1s polaritons at low temperature (Fig. S18), while two Lorentzian functions were used to fit the 2s polaritons at low temperature as well as 1s polaritons at room temperature (Figs. 2 and 3) whenever extended studies were conducted at those temperatures. Herein, the smaller q values for the 2s exciton and the photonic mode coupled to it may be due to the reduced overlap between the background broad F-P mode and the exciton and the photonic modes at the 2s exciton energy, respectively. For clarity, we have explicitly indicated in each series of measurements what functional dependence was used to fit the reflectivity spectra.

To explore the stability of Rydberg polaritons, we analysed their magneto-optical properties, as shown in Figs. 3c, S19 for 2s Rydberg and 1s ground exciton polaritons, respectively. Based on perturbation theory within low magnetic fields, the Rabi splitting under non-zero magnetic field, ΩRef(B), is given by: ΩRef(B) ≈ ΩRef(0) + a · (μB · B/R*)2/4, with a a coefficient related to the exciton wavefunction and R* the effective Rydberg constant19. Compared to 1s ground states, 2s excitonic states exhibit relatively weaker binding energy and are thus more sensitive to external magnetic fields and suffer stronger modifications of their relative electron-hole wavefunction (Fig. S20) for the same magnetic field. Indeed, Fig. 3d indicates a faster quadratic increase with magnetic field of ΩRef(B) for 2s Rydberg polaritons than for 1s polaritons, illustrating the expected stronger modification of the coupling strength for 2s polaritons. Eventually, ΩRef(B) could be enhanced by 9% and by up to 14% for 1s polaritons and 2s Rydberg polaritons at 9 T, respectively. It should be noted that even though the magnetic field could induce a Zeeman splitting of the bare WS2 excitons and, therefore, a broadening of the excitonic and polaritonic linewidths and in turn a reduction of the Rabi splitting, 1s and 2s exciton polaritons in the 1D PhC do show a clear enhancement of the Rabi splitting with increasing magnetic field, which is promising for magneto-optical polaritonic devices.

Nonlinearity of PhC 1s and 2s exciton polaritons
To quantify the nonlinearity of 1s and 2s exciton polaritons in device 1 we utilize a picosecond supercontinuum white light source (see “Methods”), enabling the coverage of the whole spectral range defined by 1s and 2s polaritons. Herein, two different experimental configurations are employed to assess the nonlinear interactions between the two different excitonic species: 1) in the first configuration, 1s and 2s polaritons are simultaneously pumped with a broadband (BB) source and, therefore, we can expect nonlinear interaction between 1s-1s polaritons, 2s-2s polaritons as well as 1s-2s polaritons; 2) in the second configuration, 1s polaritons are resonantly pumped with a narrow band (NB) source, enabling the measurement of the 1s-1s nonlinear interaction independently of higher excited state excitonic contributions.

In the BB configuration, upon increasing the pump power density from 5.0 × 10−4 mW μm−2 to 2.8 mW μm−2, the Rabi splitting between the LP and UP gradually decreases, as shown in Figs. 4a, S21 for 2s Rydberg and 1s exciton polaritons. Figure S22 shows the pump power-dependent LP and UP mode energies, and Fig. 4b shows the corresponding power density dependent differential Rabi splitting, ΩRef(N)/ΩRef(0). It is observed that for 1s exciton polaritons, ΩRef(N) under 0.46 mW μm−2 pumping intensity is equal to 90% of ΩRef(0), while for 2s exciton polaritons a transition into the weak-coupling regime is observed above 0.18 mW μm−2 (ΩRef(N) = 0.83 ΩRef(0)), based on the criterion ΩRef < (γexc + γcav)/2.

Increasing the polariton density not only decreases the Rabi splitting (2ΔEsat), due to phase space filling, but also blueshifts both polariton modes (ΔEee), due to the exchange interaction of excitons17,44,51. In our configuration, we find that the LP (UP) blueshifts (redshifts) 1.4 meV (1.5 meV) for 2s exciton polaritons under 0.18 mW μm−2 pumping power density and LP (UP) blueshifts (redshifts) 1.7 meV (1.3 meV) for 1s exciton polaritons under 0.46 mW μm−2 pumping power density. At relatively low power densities (5.0 × 10−4 mW μm−2 to 0.18 mW μm−2), phase space filling is the predominant polariton-polariton interaction mechanism, which is verified by the equal shift of UP and LP in 2s polaritons. Such an effect inhibits the simultaneous occupation of the same state within the blockade radius (Rb) based on the Pauli exclusion principle, and it results in a reduction of the oscillator strength as well as of the coupling strength, as fewer polaritons can be generated effectively46,52–54. Further increasing the power density fills the phase space of polaritons within Rb and leads to saturation. As a result, the polariton interaction potential beyond Rb starts to become significant, causing an overall blueshift in the polariton modes (ΔEee), which is verified by the unequal shift of UP and LP in 1s polaritons. Herein, ΔEsat and ΔEee could be calculated as: ΔEsat = (ΔELP + ΔEUP)/2 and ΔEee = (ΔELP − ΔEUP)/243. Because exchange interaction becomes sizeable at much larger polariton densities (~10 times larger densities than when phase space filling effects become important, Fig. S23), we only discuss the ΔEsat term in the main text.

In the NB configuration, for which we solely pump 1s polaritons, the ΩRef(N) was reduced by 9.3% at the maximum pumping power density of 0.45 mW μm−2 (Fig. S22). Under this configuration, the UP branch of 1s exciton polaritons redshifts 1.1 meV while the LP branch blueshifts 1.5 meV. Note that as the pump power increases, under both BB and NB pumping conditions, the fitted q values for the three Fano contributions reproducing the dispersion of 1s exciton polaritons start to decrease (Fig. S22) at the onset of the resonances’ spectral shifts. Overall, the nonlinear evolution of the polariton energies is thus accompanied by a reduction of the oscillator strength of 1s excitons (q for 1s exciton reduces and FWHM increases), which reduces the Rabi splitting and is consistent with exciton-exciton induced dephasing as previously characterized in TMDs monolayers55.

To quantify the different polariton-polariton interaction strengths for phase-space filling effect (ΔEsat) and of the excitonic species involved therein (1s-1s, 2s-2s, and 1s-2s), we model our polariton system as follows. For a given particle density, we can express the energy shift of each polariton branch associated to 2s and 1s polaritons as a function of the exciton/photon fraction and of the polariton population-dependent phase space filling term43,56, considering an unpolarized pump laser that generates both Y-polarized excitons and X-polarized polaritons (Supplementary Note 3): C1s/2s = X1s/2s in Eqs. (1)-(4) are all 0.5. Eventually, the extracted nonlinearity constants are 49 ± 12, 13 ± 6, and 4.9 ± 0.8 μeV μm2 for gsat2s-2s, gsat2s-1s, and gsat1s-1s in device 1, which exhibit the record values among PhC-based polaritons (Table S3). According to previous literature, the polariton–polariton interaction strength is proportional to the square of the Bohr radius and the Rabi splitting17, i.e., gxx ∝ aB2 Ω. Therefore, the enhancement that one could expect by using 2s polaritons compared to 1s polaritons is given by aB2(2s) Ω2s / aB2(1s) Ω1s = (3.8)2 16.7 / 35 = 7, which is in agreement with the experimental results (about 10 times). A more accurate value can be obtained by pumping 1s and 2s polaritons independently under NB conditions, which enables to extract two independent values of gsat2s-2s and gsat1s-1s. This methodology was applied to a second hBN/WS2/PhC structure (device 2), with the results shown in Figs. S24, S25 in the Supplementary Materials. The analysis of the data provides thus a set of interaction constants, 48.2 ± 6.7 and 8.2 ± 0.9 μeV μm2 for gsat2s-2s and gsat1s-1s, respectively, under NB pumping conditions. These values are comparable to those in device 1. Combining these values with the energy shifts measured under BB pumping in the same structure, we obtain 14.4 ± 6.8 μeV μm2 for gsat2s-1s, which is in good agreement with the theoretical prediction. Overall, the values of nonlinearity enhancement between 2s and 1s polariton as well as the gsat1s-2s interaction constant in both devices are comparable considering the error bars.

While the values of gsat2s-2s and gsat1s-1s for our TMD monolayer are in good agreement with previous reports on TMD-based polaritons, the use of a PhC instead of a vertical microcavity modifies the actual picture. In order to determine the differences in terms of polariton-polariton interactions due to the differences in the electric field distribution between the vertical cavity case and the PhC, we simulated the value of the blueshift for the two via developing a non-linear Bloch-Maxwell FDTD algorithm (Methods), and assuming that gsat for 2s and 1s are 1.36 and 0.34 μeV μm2 in the vertical dual-DBR cavity configuration (using a nonlinearity ratio of 4 from ref. 17). We first quantify the polariton population and its spatial distribution in real space, as well as its dispersion in momentum space; then we obtain the energy shift of UP and LP polaritons in a vertical DBR-based microcavity as a function of pump power. The simulated polariton population as well as the energy shift of each UP and LP peak are used as the benchmarks for comparing the nonlinearity in PhC structures. Considering comparable polariton populations in the DBR-based and the PhC-based microcavities, our simulations indicate that saturation is 15% larger for the 2s excitons and 20% larger for the 1s excitons in the corresponding PhC structures due to the spatial localization of polaritons (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Note 4). As the non-linear coefficients in the Bloch equations are chosen arbitrarily, the ΔE values are only available to compare the ratio between different systems considered. Further systematic simulation of the PhC geometry would be necessary to optimize the nonlinearity enhancement.

Finally, we notice that the nonlinearity of the 2s polaritons in our WS2-PhC structure is slightly smaller than the one measured in a vertical microcavity using three WS2 monolayers (ref. 17). The discrepancy of the calculated nonlinearity may result from several factors: 1) the assumption in ref. 17 that the contribution of the 1s polariton-2s polariton interaction to the measured spectral shifts is negligible, which we have shown to be not; 2) the difference in cavity geometry, which can affect the estimation accuracy of the absorbed number of photons and, thus, of the actual particles density (our structure lacks a top mirror and we assume full absorption at the device surface, neglecting scattering losses by the PhC structure, overestimating the number of polaritons).
paper_content.methods:
Sample preparation
The demonstrated SiN layer and 1.2 μm SiO2 were grown by low-pressure chemical vapor deposition onto Si substrate. The SiN photonic crystal is then fabricated via e-beam lithography and reactive ion etching. The thin hBN layer and monolayer WS2 were obtained by mechanical exfoliation of the bulk counterparts from 2D semiconductor and then dry transferred onto the as-fabricated 1D PhC via polycarbonate film. The 1D PhC grating parameters are listed in Fig. S1.

Optical experiments
RT angle-resolved PL and reflectance are obtained via a home-built 4f Fourier-space imaging into an Andor spectrometer (SR-500i). An 80× objective with a numerical aperture of 0.75 was used to construct the confocal system for excitation and collection. A 532 nm continuous-wave laser was utilized to excite the sample to obtain the PL. A linear polarizer and a half-waveplate were put into the collecting path to obtain the polarization-dependent angle-resolved spectra. Cryogenic temperature angle-resolved PL and reflectance are built based on Attodry 1000 (Attocube, Inc.), and the detailed schematic diagram for the setup is shown in Fig. S30. A 50× objective with a numerical aperture of 0.8 was used. The spectra are collected into a Princeton Instruments spectrometer with a cooled charge-coupled camera. For the nonlinearity, a supercontinuum pulsed light source (AnYang Laser, YSL, SC-PRO, repetition rate 0.01–80 MHz, pulse duration 100 ps) was utilized to realize two pump frameworks via long-pass and short-pass filters.

Fitting the reflectance spectra of the excitonic and polaritonic species
Due to the interference between the discrete exciton state and a continuum of states, a Fano resonance arises for the PhC cavity mode, which can be described by31:

F(E) = (q + (E − E0)/2γ)2 / 1 + ((E − E0)/2γ)2 (5)

with E the energy, E0 the exciton resonance energy, γ representing the resonance linewidth, and q the Fano factor, which describes the asymmetry of the lineshape. As the bare 1s exciton at RT and 2s exciton at 4 K show a symmetric lineshape with a close-to-zero q Fano parameter, we utilize two Lorentzian functions to obtain the polaritonic UP and LP peak positions. For 1s exciton and polariton at 4 K, we utilize one Fano lineshape to obtain the bare exciton positions and three Fano lineshapes, i.e., bare exciton background, UP and LP peaks, to fit the Fano-type polaritonic reflectance spectra (Fig. S13 and Supplementary Note 2). For the temperature-dependent analysis of the bare excitonic reflectance spectra (Figs. S14, S17), we have used Fano analysis for both 1s and 2s excitons, from which we know at which temperatures we can use two Lorentzian functions to fit the reflectance spectra. For the temperature-dependent analysis of the coupling strong regime, we have used Fano analysis for 1s polaritons and two Lorentzian functions for 2s polaritons.

Calculation of polariton/exciton density
For the nonlinearity measurements, we utilized a pulsed laser with a pulse duration of 100 ps, which is longer than the exciton lifetimes of 1s and excited 2s exciton. Therefore, the pumping source can be regarded as a continuous wave laser, and we utilized the peak energy power of each pulse. The corresponding incident pulse energy can be calculated as: Epol = Pτ / Rd, where P is the pump power, τ is set as 48/50.7 fs for the 1s/2s polaritons in WS2, regarding a photon lifetime of 35 fs, R is the repetition rate of the laser, and d is the pulse duration. Then the absorbed photon by the polariton branches of the super continuum pulsed light source was estimated via the R integral of the absorption of the pumped laser profile: E(k) = Eto Rt Aabsor(k) / Alaser(k), where Aabsor(k) is the absorbed dip of the spectra at different k-vectors and Alaser(k) is intrinsic pumped laser profile. Then we can calculate the polariton density as N = E(k)/Epol Abeam, where Abeam = πD2/4 with D roughly 2.5 μm and Epol is the energy of the polaritons. As we utilize unpolarized light (with a polarization degree 20% along x direction), Y-polarized excitons (in the weak coupling regime) will also be generated (Figs. S31, S32). According to Eqs. 1–4, we included the effect of Y-polarized excitons, considering the excitonic lifetime and the bare excitonic absorption, with measured excitonic linewidths of 6.5 and 7.9 meV for 2s and 1s excitons, respectively, at 4 K.

Numerical methods
All simulations are performed using the non-linear Bloch-Maxwell FDTD57. The system we consider is similar to the experimental sample. We make use of the periodicity of the system and consider one period under periodic boundary using Bloch theorem58 along the x-direction and perfectly matched layers (PML) along the y-direction (Fig. S33) for the calculations in the linear regime. In the non-linear regime, since different k-vectors are coupled due to the exciton-exciton scattering, the Bloch theorem is no longer applicable in the framework of our algorithm, and we therefore use PMLs along both x and y directions and consider 200 grating periods.

Simulation results obtained in Fig. 1 are obtained using the total field/scattered field method58, calculating the reflectivity spectrum for each k-vector independently. We used a pulsed plane wave source with a finite k-vector, with a pulse duration 1 fs in order to excite the system broadband. In order to fit the experiment, the refractive indices have been slightly adjusted between the 4 K and RT simulations. The exciton resonances and the light-matter coupling coefficients are also adjusted to fit the experiment59 (see Supplementary materials for detailed parameters).

Simulation results obtained in Fig. 4d are obtained in the framework of the non-linear Bloch-Maxwell FDTD. We pump the system using an X-polarized plane wave CW source resonant and measure the reflectivity at the anti-crossing. We then compare the obtained dispersion to the dispersion of the bare system to obtain the blueshift. We repeat this procedure on a microcavity polariton system in order to compare the effective interaction coefficient (Figs. S34, S35).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript reported the strong coupling between 2s state of excitons and a cavity photon on a SiN waveguide. Moreover, they identified the nonlinearity of the 2s Rydberg exciton polaritons. Benefiting from the broad range of photonic band, they can compare the nonlinearity with 1s exciton polaritons simultaneously. In the end, they show the propagation properties of exciton polaritons due to the finite wavevector. The evidence of strong coupling is clear, and the characterization of nonlinearity is solid. I would like to suggest the manuscript to be published in Nature Communications if the following questions can be addressed properly.
1、I suggest the authors show the full dispersion of the photonic mode in the manuscript. considering the grating can support both guided mode resonances and the so called BIC mode.
2、 With increasing temperature, the Rabi splitting of 1s state increase from 22 meV to 35 meV, which is quite surprising to me. Could the author show a temperature dependence of the Rabi splitting and elaborate more on it?
3、The mode volume of DBR-metal cavity used in the reference 17 should be comparable with the waveguide mode used in the manuscript. Moreover, the monolayer stamped on the top of the waveguide will only interact with the evanescent wave of the mode. I am still confused how the interaction strength could be so strong.
4、It seems like the author can reproduced the experiment with FDTD simulation. The parameters are shown in the supplemental materials. The light matter coupling is described by a coefficient Omega. I am wondering the relationship between the Omega and the Rabi splitting or the coupling strength. Please clarify why Omega of 1s state used for the figure 1c and figure1d is so different. And in figure 1d, the Omega for 2s state is more than 10 times smaller than that of 1s. However, the Rabi splitting for 2s state and 1s state are not that different, which are 15 meV and 35 meV respectively.
5、The last section of the current manuscript discussed the propagation of 1s exciton polaritons, which does not seem to be relevant with the topic of the manuscript. I suggest the authors to move it to the supplemental materials.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this manuscript, Shang et al. demonstrate the first realization of on-chip Rydberg polaritons in monolayer WS2 coupled with a 1D photonic crystal (PhC) cavity structure. By leveraging the large Bohr radius of Rydberg excitons and PhC-induced field localization, the authors achieve a nonlinearity enhancement of 23 ± 10 times for 2s polaritons compared to ground-state 1s polaritons, with robust operation up to 80 K and magnetic field-tunable Rabi splitting.
The manuscript addresses a critical gap in on-chip polaritonic devices by combining monolayer TMDs with PhC engineering, yielding groundbreaking results in Rydberg polariton nonlinearity and propagation. The experimental and theoretical framework is rigorous, and the results are well-supported by angle-resolved spectroscopy and FDTD simulations. I think this manuscript is suitable for publication in Nature Communications after revision. The following comments should be addressed in detail to improve the manuscript:
(1) The introduction mentions that Rydberg excitons have large Bohr radii and are promising for enhancing optical nonlinearities. However, it is not clear how the specific properties of Rydberg excitons in monolayer WS2 compare to other materials. Could you provide more details on this?
(2) In Figure 1c and 1d, the strong coupling between the WS2 excitons and PhC modes is demonstrated. How do the specific geometric parameters of the PhC (period, width) influence the coupling strength and the resulting polariton dispersion?
(3) The temperature-dependent measurements show that the 2s exciton polaritons survive up to 80 K. What specific mechanisms cause the degradation of the strong coupling regime above this temperature, and are there any strategies to mitigate these effects?
(4) From Figure S3 in SI, it can be seen that the line widths of 1s and 2s excitons and cavity photons are different at room temperature and 4 K. Does this have an impact on the judgment of strong coupling? For example, does the narrower line width of the 2s exciton at 4 K mean a higher quality coupling to the photon mode?
(5) The propagation decay constant of the PhC polaritons is measured to be around 6.3 μm. How does this value compare to other polariton systems, and what factors limit the propagation distance in this case?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In the manuscript titled “Enhanced nonlinearity of photonic crystal Rydberg exciton polaritons in monolayer WS2”, the authors present a photonic crystal (PhC)-based on-chip polaritonic device demonstrating strong coupling between PhC modes and both the ground-state and Rydberg-state excitons of WS2. They conduct a detailed characterization of the polariton states through reflection measurements under varying magnetic field and temperature, as well as nonlinearity and propagation measurements. The key claim of the work is a 23-fold enhancement of the non-linearity associated with the Rydberg state polaritons relative to the ground state. They attribute the enhancement to the enhanced overlap of the PhC mode electric field with the excitons in the PhC geometry. The authors have also estimated the interaction constants and propagation decay constants for the ground state and excited state exciton-polaritons.
The manuscript is thorough and clearly written. The exploration of strong polaritonic effects, particularly large nonlinearity using PhCs instead of the more common Fabry-Perot cavities, is of potential interest. However, I have several comments that should be addressed before recommending publication:
1. Reference 17, which probed nonlinearity of WSe2 embedded in a Fabry-Perot cavity, reported that the interaction for the 2s exciton-polaritons is 4.6 times stronger than for the 1s exciton-polaritons. While the current study finds a similar nonlinearity for 2s exciton-polaritons, it reports a 23-fold suppression for 1s exciton-polaritons. Direct comparison is difficult due to differences in geometry and photon absorption estimates, yet this discrepancy is notable. It is not clear how this difference (with respect to cavity geometry) can result from “the combination of an extended exciton radius due to the excited-state nature of the employed excitons, and to the PhC-induced spatial field localization.” Since this is a key point in the abstract, the authors should clarify their explanation.
2. Building on the previous comment, the title is somewhat misleading – it seems to suggest that using a PhC (instead of a traditional Fabry-Perot cavity) enhances the nonlinearity. However, the authors themselves note that the extracted nonlinearity constants align with previous studies. I recommend revising the title to more accurately reflect the findings
3. The focus of the paper is somewhat diluted. It is unclear how the propagation measurement supports the central claim of the paper.
4. In the temperature-dependent measurements (Figure 2c), the coupling strength of 2s excitons decreases monotonically, while 1s excitons maintain a nearly constant coupling strength. Could the authors provide further insight into this monotonic decrease for 2s excitons?
5. In the magnetic field-dependent measurements (Figure 2d), the coupling strength exhibits quadratic enhancement with the magnetic field, but this enhancement is not symmetric around zero field, particularly for 2s excitons. Could the authors clarify the origin of this asymmetry?
6. In the nonlinearity measurements, the authors have performed experiments in two configurations, viz., the broadband (BB) pumping of both the 1s and 2s states, and a narrow band (NB) pumping of the 1s states alone. Therefore, the authors could effectively compare the interactions between the various types of excitonic states. To further probe the role of the Rydberg excitons, I suggest an additional experiment where 2s excitons are resonantly pumped, analogous to the narrowband 1s excitation. While phonon assisted relaxation to the 1s state could still occur, this measurement could provide valuable insights into the intrinsic 2s-2s interactions.
7. Determining whether the system is in the strong or weak coupling regime requires accurate extraction of the bare exciton energy and linewidth. How do the authors obtain these values? Do they use the same device with different polarization of light?
8. The authors use dashed guidelines to indicate the energy values of LP and UP in several figures. Accurate extraction of these values is crucial for assessing temperature dependence, magnetic field dependence, Rabi splitting, nonlinearity, etc. How are the LP and UP energies determined? Could the authors elaborate on their extraction/fitting method? That is important since in some cases, e.g., in Fig. S10, the energy shift is not prominent.
9. Could the authors further elaborate on the rationale behind Equations (1–4) in the main text? For example, it is unclear why the 1s-2s terms contributing to the energy shift of 2s excitons depend on N_1s but not on N_2s.
10. The propagation experiment methodology is unclear. Why do the authors block certain regions (white rectangles) in the angle-resolved spectra? With the full spectrum available, they could simply select the desired energy and angle range for integration. Additionally, how do they physically block specific energy ranges in the actual experiment?
11. In Figure 4e, the PL intensity decay for the exciton polaritons at energies of 2.11 and 2.15 eV are plotted. However, as observed in Figure 1b and discussed towards the beginning of the Results section, the reflectance data of the bare cavity is dominated by Fabry-Perot modes corresponding to the underlying thick SiO2 layer between 2.10-2.14 eV. How did the authors distinguish the exciton-polariton features despite the strong Fabry-Perot oscillations?
12. Previous studies have explored excitons in TMDCs using 1D photonic crystals (e.g., L. Zhang et al., Nat. Commun. 9, 713 (2018)). Could the authors comment on how their approach differs in any significant way? Additionally, could they include dispersion data for the bare cavity across the full range of measured angles in the SI?
13. Unlike Fabre-Perot cavity, 1d PhCs has additional anisotropy. Could the authors comment whether this anisotropy affects exciton-polariton properties and their nonlinearity?

reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
The work reports on the experimental investigation and theoretical interpretation of Rydberg polaritons in one-dimensional (1D) photonic crystal lattices. In particular, a WS2 monolayer is deposited, with a 15 nm buffer of hBN, on top of a 220 nm thick 1D-grating in SiN sitting on a glass (SiO2) cladding. Optical excitations are probed in reflectance spectroscopy. This result is, per se, not novel. Exciton-polaritons have been reported in similar settings (actually, from the very same two-dimensional semiconductor, WS2, coupled to a SiN photonic crystal, with a two-dimensional lattice, instead of a simpler 1D one), see, e.g., Nano Letters vol. 20, 5292 (2020).
The Rabi splitting in the order of 20 meV reported in these works is compatible, which is good to begin with, but not sufficient to claim a significant innovation as a result. In addition, polariton linewidths are extremely large in the experiment reported here, roughly of the same magnitude as the Rabi splitting basically, which makes the strong coupling hardly distinguished from the measurements, in fact. This is actually much worse than what was shown in the quoted Nano Letters. The authors may want to give an interpretation on this. Looking at the spectra of Figs. 1 and 2, one might actually even doubt that the sample is in the strong coupling regime, was not for a clever lineshape fit.
In any case, going further than the linear polariton physics, the authors explore the coupling between excited Rydberg states from the WS2 monolayer excitonic response to the same photonic eigenmode of the 1D photonic lattice. The experimental evidence points towards an enhanced nonlinear response of the 2s-related exciton polariton as compared to the 1s-related one. In particular, the 2s-2s nonlinearity is quantified to be (with large exp error, though) more than 20 times larger as compared to the 1s-1s. This result might be considered as an interesting one, per se, since it justifies current interest in exploring Rydberg polariton physics for various applications. However, also in this case the result cannot be considered as completely unexpected or novel. In fact, as also acknowledged in the manuscript large nonlinearities for the 2s-related exciton polaritons were already reported in Nat. Comm. vol. 12, 2269 (2021), albeit in a vertical microcavity geometry.
authors shuold make sure that when exciting the system with the pulsed pump, any excitation of the exciton reservoir can be neglected, otherwose the estimat eof the nonlinear might be inaccurate
Here the authors also report estimates for the polariton propagation constant, which is obtained from non-resonant excitation experiments in the few microns range. Also in this case, while it may be considered one of the first experiments showing Rydberg polariton propagation in WS2 monolayers, much longer polariton propagation distances have been already shown in alternative materials, so also in this case I feel very reluctant to recommend publication in Nature Communications, in the absence of a stronger argument justifying the novelty of this work as compared to the literature. Honestly, the linewidths of these polaritons are really broad, and thus losses must be huge. What are the reasons for that? The authors could elaborate a bit more on this aspect, and try to figure out mitigation strategies, if any. In fact, I would expect resonant modes from the underlying SiN grating to display much narrower lines (notice that a photon lifetime of 35 fs quoted in methods...this is really short for a dielectric grating!), thus affecting the overall polariton losses.
In conclusion, while the experimental results reported in this work, as well as the agreement with numerical simulations based on the nonlinear finite-difference time-domain method, seem to be well conceived and reported, the overall novelty and main claims of enhanced figure of merits as compared to the literature are not sufficiently sufficiently justified or groundbreaking to be published in Nature Communications. There are certain elements of novelty that deserve publication of these results, but I would still consider them as incremental and, as such, suited to a more specialized journal in condensed matter physics, not necessarily belonging to the Springer Nature group. As it stands, I would feel very reluctant to reconsider this work for publication here, in the absence of a truly game changing result based on these materials.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to Reviewers (NCOMMS-25-13902A)
Reply to Reviewer 1
General Comment:
The manuscript reported the strong coupling between 2s state of excitons and a cavity photon on a SiN waveguide. Moreover, they identified the nonlinearity of the 2s Rydberg exciton polaritons. Benefiting from the broad range of photonic band, they can compare the nonlinearity with 1s exciton polaritons simultaneously. In the end, they show the propagation properties of exciton polaritons due to the finite wavevector. The evidence of strong coupling is clear, and the characterization of nonlinearity is solid. I would like to suggest the manuscript to be published in Nature Communications if the following questions can be addressed properly.
Response:
We sincerely thank the referee for the favorable evaluation of our work and for summarizing clearly the main achievements of our work. We wish to express our deep gratitude and respect for reviewing our manuscript.
Herein, we would like to point out that, due to reviewers 3&4 and 5 questioning on the analysis of the reflectance spectra, to obtain the polaritons' spectral position, we have fitted all reflectance spectra again with Fano functions. Furthermore, due to reviewers 3&4 and 5 questioning on the effect of optical and excitonic anisotropies on the measured nonlinearities, we have revised equations 1-4 of the main text to take into account cross-polarized contributions to the polariton nonlinearity. Based on this new formulation, we have reanalyzed the data (device 1) shown in the first version of the manuscript (Figure 4) as well as a new series of measurements on a second identical structure (device 2) fabricated for answering some of the questions raised during the revision of the article (Figure S24 and S25). See details in comment 13 to reviewer 3 and comment 3 to reviewer 5. The two structures give consistent values for the Rabi splittings and nonlinearities.
Comment 1:
I suggest the authors show the full dispersion of the photonic mode in the manuscript. considering the grating can support both guided mode resonances and the so called BIC mode.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the suggestion on comprehensively clarifying the full dispersion of the bare photonic modes. As shown in Figure R1a and b, the X-polarized bound state in the continuum (BIC) mode appears at zero wavevector and at an energy of ~2.11 eV.
Given the large detuning between the BIC mode and the 1s exciton, the coupling happens rather between the excitonic mode and the photonic branches at a nonzero wavevector that end up forming the BIC mode at zero wavevector. For completeness, we have explored the coupling between these photonic branches and the 1s excitons. Figure R1b and c display a zoom-in into the polaritons' dispersion around the corresponding energies and wavevectors. The detailed angle-resolved reflectance spectra near the anti-crossing area are shown in Figure R1d. The angle-resolved reflectance spectra are fitted via a three-Fano lineshape function (see comment 2 for details) to obtain the peak positions of the upper polariton branch (UP) and lower polariton branch (LP). Further, the obtained peak positions are fitted with a coupled-oscillator model (Figure R1e), which indicates a coupling strength Ω of 38 ± 3 meV, larger than (gamma_exc + gamma_cav)/2 = (8.9+24)/2 = 16.5 meV, which ensures the system is in the strong coupling regime. Not surprisingly, this coupling strength is very close to the one observed for the photonic mode coupled with the 1s exciton at 4 K that is analyzed in the main manuscript.
Based on the reviewer’s suggestion (as well as comment 12 of reviewer 3), we have updated Figure 1 in the main text and presented an overview of our cavity properties, as shown in Figure R2 below. To highlight the full dispersion of the photonic modes and indicate explicitly the position of the BIC mode, we added the corresponding polariton dispersions at 4 K (Figure R1) into the supplementary information, illustrating the formation of polaritons with these additional photonic modes.
Figure R1. Full dispersion of the X-polarized photonic modes, including a BIC mode.
a, The full dispersion of the X-polarized photonic modes with monolayer WS and hBN 2 on top, displaying a BIC mode around 2.1 eV at null wavevector. b, Zoomed-in polariton dispersion at 4 K of 1s exciton coupled to the photonic branch leading to the BIC mode. c, Replotted b after subtracting the signal at k=0. d, The detailed angle-resolved reflectance spectra in c for X-polarized BIC near the anti-crossing area (white dashed boxes in b and c). e. Fitting of the UP and LP peak positions with a coupled-oscillator model indicates a coupling strength of 38 ± 3 meV. f, The corresponding photonic and excitonic fractions of UP and LP for X-polarized photonic mode coupling with 1s exciton whose dispersion is shown in (e).
Figure R2. Demonstration of as-fabricated X-polarized photonic mode. a, A schematic diagram of PhC dressed Rydberg exciton polariton based on a hybrid hBN/WS /PhC structure. b, The experimental angle-resolved reflectance spectra for X-polarized modes of the bare PhC structure with hBN but without monolayer WS on top. Two black dashed lines indicate the energy for the 1s and 2s excitons at 4 K, while the red dashed circles indicate the regions around zero detuning. c, Middle two panels: the simulated electric-field profile in the y−z plane for X-polarized mode 1 at the targeted angles and energies (red circles in b) for the hBN/PhC structure, considering an hBN thickness of 15 nm. Side two panels: The corresponding integrated electric-field intensity across one unit cell for the 1s and 2s exciton wavelengths, indicating that the electric-field intensity at the WS position (black dashed lines) is 0.8 and 0.6 times that of the maximum electric field intensity across the whole structure for 1s and 2s excitons, respectively.

Line 147, page 7, main text: added “Note that the as-designed 1D PhC can not only support guided mode resonances but also a so-called bound state in the continuum (BIC) mode at a wavevector equal to zero (Fig. S11), although in our study it does not couple to either of the excitonic resonances. However, the photonic branches leading to the BIC mode indeed do couple, with a coupling strength Ω of 38 ± 3 meV, with the 1s excitons at 4 K and at a nonzero wavevector.”

Comment 2:
With increasing temperature, the Rabi splitting of 1s state increase from 22 meV to 35 meV, which is quite surprising to me. Could the author show a temperature dependence of the Rabi splitting and elaborate more on it?
Response:
Actually, the Rabi splitting for the 1s exciton polariton decreases when going from low temperature (35 meV) to room-temperature (25 meV). Our actual statement was: “In addition, the X-polarized mode 1 also couples to 1s exciton states with an energy separation of 35.0 ± 3.0 meV, larger than at RT due to the narrowing of the excitonic line”. Herein, we have followed the reviewer's suggestion and provided now a thorough study of the temperature-dependent strong coupling of 1s state exciton polaritons in WS . We have thus fabricated a new photonic crystal device (device 2) onto which we have transferred again hBN and WS and performed therein the temperature dependence dispersion measurements. Figure R3 presents the temperature dependent reflectance spectra around the 1s exciton energy from 295 K to 15 K. Since the bare exciton absorption line (accessible typically at large angles) can be distinguished in each spectrum, we could extract the bare exciton energy and linewidth of the 1s exciton for each temperature. The corresponding reflectance spectra of the 1s exciton for all temperatures are shown in Figure R4a. Each reflectance spectrum is fitted with an asymmetric Fano lineshape function due to the interference between the discrete 1s exciton state and a continuum of states (Nat. Commun. 9, 713 (2018)):
F(E) = (q +(E -E0)/2gamma)^2 / 1+(E -E0)/2gamma)^2 (1)
with E the energy, E0 the exciton resonance energy, gamma representing the resonance linewidth, and q the Fano factor, which describes the asymmetry of the lineshape.
Figure R3. Temperature dependent reflectance spectra around 1s exciton for device 2 from 295 K to 15 K.
The extracted peak energy and the linewidth for the 1s exciton versus temperature are shown in Figure R4b and c. As temperature decreases, the peak position blue shifts from 2.028 to 2.086 eV, which is due to the reduction in electron-phonon interactions and an increase in the band gap at lower temperatures (Nano Lett. 21, 6240-6246 (2024)). In the same temperature range, the linewidth decreases from 24.8 to 7.0 meV, which is ascribed to the decreased scattering of excitons with phonons (Nat. Commun. 7, 13279 (2016)).
Figure R4. Temperature dependent reflectance spectra of 1s exciton in device 2 from 15 K to 295 K at large angles (a), the fitted peak position (b), and linewidth (c).
Figure R5. Temperature dependent Rabi splitting for 1s polariton and (gamma_exc + gamma_cav)/2.
Subsequently, we extracted the Rabi splitting for each temperature from Figure R3 and plotted it in Figure R5. The Rabi splitting is larger than (gamma_exc + gamma_cav)/2 at each temperature, ensuring that the system operates in the strong coupling regime from 15 K to 295 K. One can observe that the Rabi splitting is roughly constant (32-35 meV) from low temperatures up to about 200 K, consistent with an almost constant excitonic broadening (7-9 meV). As temperature increases further, the Rabi splitting decreases from 35 ± 3 to 25 ± 2 meV, while the linewidth of the 1s exciton increases from 9 to 25 meV due to enhanced electron phonon coupling and an acceleration of the exciton dephasing (Nat. Commun. 9, 713 (2018)). Interestingly, the two studied devices (the one analyzed in the main manuscript and the new one fabricated for answering the reviewers’ question) display the same quantitative values (~35 meV at low temperatures for both devices, and 25 meV at room-temperature), confirming the robustness of the photonic crystal fabrication and the quality and reproducibility of the hBN/WS transfer.
Based on the reviewer’s suggestion, we have added a discussion where we present the temperature dependent Rabi splitting in the main text and put Figure R3-5 into the supplementary information to present the corresponding results.

Comment 3:
The mode volume of DBR-metal cavity used in the reference 17 should be comparable with the waveguide mode used in the manuscript. Moreover, the monolayer stamped on the top of the waveguide will only interact with the evanescent wave of the mode. I am still confused how the interaction strength could be so strong.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this interesting question that will allow us to clarify the large interaction strength in our PhC configuration, which has been scarcely exploited compared to the standard vertical cavity configuration. If, for the moment, we obviate the difference in active material (WSe in Ref. 17 and WS in our case), the main difference in coupling strength will originate from the distinct exciton-electric field overlap between the two structures. Figure 4a of the Supplementary Material of Ref. 17 shows the calculated photonic field distribution along with the position of the WSe layers in the structure studied in Ref. 17. It should be noted that the WSe monolayers are not positioned at the antinodes of the electric field distribution, but rather between an antinode and a secondary maximum, leading to a coupling between the active material and the photonic field that does not attain its potential maximum, but rather just 40% of the potential maximum. This leads to a smaller Rabi splitting than what can be expected if the monolayers were located at the maximum of the photonic field. In our system, contrary to what one could initially think, the active layers are indeed positioned close to the maximum of the electric field, as can be seen in Figure R2c (now Figure 1c) of our main manuscript.
To provide a more accurate comparison, we would ideally need to compare our structure with a vertical microcavity with the same active layer as ours and in which the monolayers are located at the maximum of the electric field intensity distribution. To do so, we can compare, for instance, Ref 52 (Nat. Commun. 14, 1512 (2023)), where WS is also employed as an active region and located at the center of the cavity. In this case, the Rabi splitting for 1s excitons at room temperature becomes stronger, of the order of 32-35 meV, which matches consistently our Rabi splitting values.
To give a global overview of the Rabi energy of intralayer exciton-based exciton polaritons in TMDs, we present a table below where we make a comparison among representative TMD based microcavities. Within PhC based polaritons, our Rabi energy (35 meV at 4 K) is indeed comparable to previous works (17.6 to 32 meV). However, when looking into different TMD based configurations, e.g., DBR based cavity, Bloch surface wave waveguided polariton, and metal-based nanocavity, our Rabi energy at room temperature (22-25 meV) is far from being the maximum measured, even with the same active material.
Overall, the interaction strength in our case is explained by the rather optimized overlap between the WS monolayer and the electric field. To reassure the reader that this is so, new Figure 1c of the main manuscript provides the intensity of the electric field at the position of the TMD monolayer. Besides, we have included Table R1 in the supplementary information to compare quantitatively our results with those previously published.
Table R1. Comparison of Rabi energy among representative TMD based configurations.

Line 145, page 7, main text: added “Notably, by positioning the active layers close to the maximum of the electric field, our obtained Ω for both 1s and 2s polaritons are comparable with that measured in planar DBR-based microcavities, in which the monolayer is located close to an antinode of the electric field distribution (Table S2).”

Comment 4:
It seems like the author can reproduced the experiment with FDTD simulation. The parameters are shown in the supplemental materials. The light matter coupling is described by a coefficient Omega. I am wondering the relationship between the Omega and the Rabi splitting or the coupling strength. Please clarify why Omega of 1s state used for the figure 1c and figure1d is so different. And in figure 1d, the Omega for 2s state is more than 10 times smaller than that of 1s. However, the Rabi splitting for 2s state and 1s state are not that different, which are 15 meV and 35 meV respectively.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestion on clarifying the coupling coefficient. The light matter coupling coefficient, Omega’ (Ω’), that is used in the FDTD simulations, is completely independent of the distribution of the photon and exciton modes: it is a coefficient that depends solely on the exciton properties (proportional to the exciton oscillator strength). In our simulations, it is chosen as a fitting parameter (read further below), whose numerical values can be compared to those necessary to reproduce existing experimental results in literature, in particular the results of Ref 52.
More precisely, the Rabi splitting is proportional to the square root of the normalized overlap between the photonic and exciton modes, which is taking into account automatically in our FDTD calculations by the design of the simulated structure, times the light matter coupling coefficient, Ω_Ref ~(Ω’)2 *sigma_overlap (Phys. Rev. B 106, 115424 (2022); Condens. Matter Phys. 17, 23702 (2014); A. Kavokin & al. Microcavities). To illustrate this, we performed FDTD simulations of a vertical 1D microcavity where the only parameter that we modified was the value of Ω’. As shown in Figure R6, a 4-fold Ω’ increase induces a 2-fold increase of the Rabi energy, as expected.
Figure R6. 1D FDTD simulation of double-6 pairs TiO /SiO based exciton-polariton microcavity for two different values of the light matter coupling coefficient.
The difference between the Ω’ values used in Figure 1c and 1d (52 meV at 4 K to 11.2 meV at RT) can be explained by the fact that our FDTD simulations do not take into account polariton-phonon coupling. Indeed, Figure 1c and 1d show that the Rabi splitting decreases from 35 (at 4 K) to 25 (at RT) meV, which is mainly due to the exciton dephasing resulting from phonon scattering as temperature increases (Nat. Commun. 9, 713 (2018)). As the only free parameters in our FDTD simulations are the spatially (and spectrally) varying refractive index distribution, which defines the photonic structure, and the excitonic resonance properties, defined by the exciton resonance energy and Ω’. To account for the reduction in Rabi splitting by polariton-phonon interaction, we need to modify Ω’ (for each temperature the exciton energy is taken from the experimental reflectivity measurements, and it is thus fixed). As explained in the previous paragraph, a reduction of Rabi splitting is necessarily accompanied in our model by a reduction of Ω’.
For the ratio between Ω’ for 1s and 2s states, a ratio of 3.8 for the square roots of the simulated omegas (52 meV for 1s and 3.7 meV for 2s) is found, which is comparable with previous works (2.3 - 3.2 in Nat. Commun. 12, 2269 (2021)). Let us first remind the criterion for strong coupling, i.e., Ω > (gamma_exc + gamma_cav)/2. To analyze its dependence on temperature, one must thus monitor the homogeneous exciton broadening as a function of temperature (assuming that the refractive index for the cavity is temperature independent). The temperature dependence of the 2s exciton linewidth is shown in Figure R10. The reflectance spectrum is fitted with an asymmetric Fano line shape function due to the interference between the discrete 2s exciton state and a continuum of states (Nat. Commun. 9, 713 (2018)):
F(E) = (q +(E -E0)/2gamma)^2 / 1+(E -E0)/2gamma)^2 (4)
with E the energy, E0 the exciton resonance energy, gamma representing the resonance linewidth, and q the Fano factor, which describes the asymmetry of the lineshape. The fitted q values are shown in Figure R10b, which are all below 0.08, indicating 2s excitons exhibit a symmetric lineshape close to a Lorentz oscillator.

The extracted peak energy and the linewidth for the 2s exciton versus temperature are shown in Figure R10c and d. As temperature increases, the peak position redshifts from 2.261 to 2.257 eV, which is due to the increase in electron-phonon interactions and a reduction of the bandgap at higher temperatures (Nano Lett. 21, 6240-6246 (2024)). Concomitantly, the linewidth increases from 7.5 to 15.0 meV, which is ascribed to the enlarged exciton scattering.
Combining the measured 2s exciton broadening (Figure R10d) with the fitting of the reflectance spectra as a function of temperature shown in Figure 3a of the main text (Figure R11a), which provides the Rabi splitting as a function of temperature, we can now plot all the quantities involved and verify the Ω > (gamma_exc + gamma_cav)/2 criterion as a function of temperature. As shown in Figure R11b, the Rabi splitting is larger than (gamma_exc + gamma_cav)/2 up to about 80 K. Further increasing temperature prevents distinguishing LP and UP (120 K for example) due to exciton dephasing and broadening of the 2s exciton linewidth.
Overall, to mitigate this effect and sustain the strong-coupling with 2s exciton up to higher temperatures, one could either 1) reduce the linewidth of monolayer WS 2s excitons by minimizing their broadening; people usually utilize hBN encapsulation or annealing to improve the excitonic linewidth (Phys. Rev. Applied 14, 021002 (2020)); 2) optimize the linewidth of the cavity mode via refining the fabrication process of the cavity or by using photonic modes displaying intrinsically larger quality factors, such as BIC (Nature 605, 447–452 (2022)), which in principle have an infinite lifetime.

Thus, the narrower the excitonic linewidth, the easier to fulfill the previous criterion for a given cavity photon linewidth (gamma_cav). However, the principal quantum number also affects the oscillator strength and, thus, the left-hand side of the criterion.
Moreover, since the coupling strength between excitons and photonic modes also depends on the overlap between the excitonic wavefunction and the electric field distribution, one should also take into account the effect of potentially unequal overlaps (which is our case). This overlap is given by ∫Ψ_exc(r)Ψ_cav(r)d3r, with Ψ_exc(r) and Ψ_cav(r) the exciton and photon wavefunction. If we assume 1s and 2s exciton wavefunctions based on hydrogen-like wavefunctions (which are certainly an approximation for TMD-based excitons):
Ψ_1s(r) = 1/sqrt(pi*aB^3) * exp(-r/aB) (5)
Ψ_2s(r) = 1/sqrt(8*pi*aB^3) * (1-r/2aB) * exp(-r/2aB) (6)
a being the exciton Bohr radii. Taking into account that within aB the photon field can be considered as a constant (0.6 and 0.8 for 1s and 2s excitons, Figure R2c), we could calculate the overlap between the photonic and exciton modes as:
1s: ∫ 0 aB Ψ_1s(r)Ψ_cav(r)d3r ≈ A * ∫ 0 aB 1/sqrt(pi*aB^3) * exp(-r/aB) d3r ≈ 0.91*(aB)^3/2
2s: ∫ 0 aB Ψ_2s(r)Ψ_cav(r)d3r ≈ B * ∫ 0 aB 1/sqrt(8*pi*aB^3) * (1-r/2aB) * exp(-r/2aB) d3r ≈ 0.22*(aB)^3/2
Considering the Bohr radii of 1.8 nm for the 1 s state and 6.6 nm for the 2 s state, as in WSe (Nat. Commun. 12, 2269 (2021)), we could calculate the ratio between the overlap integrals overlap_1s/overlap_2s ≈ 0.58. Similarly, if we consider an overlap across a distance of 2aB, the ratio will be 0.89. Thus, depending on whether we consider aB or 2aB for the spatial extension of the overlap, the ratios are 2.2 or 3.4, similar to our calculated and measured Rabi energies. In this sense, the coupling strength of 2s excitons is “extrinsically” enhanced compared to that of 1s excitons due to a better exciton-photonic mode overlap at the energy of the 2s exciton. This enhancement reinforces the effect of the larger spatial extension of the 2s exciton wavefunction.

Response:
We thank the reviewer’s interest for their interest in the propagation of polaritons. Let us remind first that the propagation decay constant (D) is proportional to the group velocity (v) and the polariton lifetime (tau_pol), which in turn depends on the excitonic/photonic fraction of the considered polaritons i.e., the position along the polariton dispersion (Nat. Nanotechnol. 13, 906-909 (2018)). v can be calculated from the experimental dispersions as v = dE/dk*hbar, while tau_pol can be calculated from 1/tau_pol = X/tau_EX + C/tau_P, if both the exciton lifetime (tau_EX) and the photon lifetime (tau_P) are known. Since in most polariton systems the excitonic lifetime is much larger than the photonic lifetime, the polariton lifetime is mostly limited by the photonic lifetime, which would push to exploit more excitonic-like polaritons. However, the larger the excitonic fraction, the smaller the group velocity and, thus, for each material system and cavity structure, a compromise between group velocity and polariton lifetime needs to be found. In general, longer propagation lengths are found for more photonic-like polaritons, showing that larger group velocities over larger polariton lifetimes are favored. In this context, maximizing the photonic lifetime is thus a must, as indicated explicitly in the main text.
The propagation decay constant (6.3 m) measured in our work is comparable to previous reported TMD based polariton systems, as listed in the Table R3.

F(E) = (q +(E -E0)/2gamma)^2 / 1+(E -E0)/2gamma)^2 (10)
with E the energy, E0 the resonance energy, gamma representing the resonance linewidth, and q the Fano factor, which describes the asymmetry of the lineshape. Therefore, to fit and extract the actual polariton position, we considered Fano-type polaritonic reflectance spectra for 1s polaritons, consisting of three Fano contributions, i.e., bare exciton background, UP and LP peaks, and two Lorentz functions for 2s exciton polaritons (UP and LP peaks) at low temperature. Meanwhile, for the temperature-dependent study of bare excitons (see comment 4), we performed the analysis of 1s and 2s exciton species with Fano resonances. We can now compare the nonlinearity extracted from our experimental data, as well as that reported in reference 17, with the expected nonlinearity enhancement due exclusively to the unequal Bohr radii of different Rydberg polaritons. In the simplest picture, the polariton–polariton interaction strength is proportional to the square of the Bohr radius and the Rabi splitting, i.e., g_xx ∝ aB^2 * Omega. Therefore, the enhancement one could expect by using 2s polaritons compared to 1s polaritons is given by (aB_2s^2 * Omega_2s) / (aB_1s^2 * Omega_1s) = (3.66/3.8)^2 * 15/35 = 5.7/6.5, considering a Bohr radii ratio of 3.66 (Nat. Commun. 12, 2269 (2021)) or 3.8 (Nano Lett. 20, 7635−7641 (2020)), respectively.
Next, we can add into our considerations the enhancement of polariton-polariton nonlinear interactions due to the unequal field distribution in PhC and vertical microcavities (formed by two DBRs). For the comparison, we use perfectly matched layers boundary along both x and y directions and consider a 200 period PhC structure in the nonlinear Bloch-Maxwell FDTD simulation. We then pump the system using a planewave CW source and measure the reflectivity at the anticrossing area. We further quantify the polariton population and its spatial distribution by monitoring the photonic component of the polaritons (i.e., the real space distribution of the photonic electric-field profile at the energies of UP and LP for both 1s and 2s polaritons). By varying the pump power of the light source and comparing the obtained dispersion to the dispersion of the system in the linear regime, we obtain the energy shift of UP and LP polaritons, from which we deduce the nonlinearity strength (i.e., phase space filling interaction in the main text).
To compare with the planar case, we apply the same simulation procedure to a planar microcavity containing WS too and we assume that g^sat for 2s and 1s are 1.36 and 0.34 eV m2 (using a nonlinearity ratio of 4, close to the 4.6 value from Nat. Commun. 12, 2269 (2021), i.e., from reference 17). Compared to reference 17, the only difference is that in our simulation of the planar microcavity, we place the WS at the maximum of the cavity mode electric field. Figure R16 shows the polariton distribution (obtained from its photonic component) for the UP and LP polaritons associated with 1s and 2s excitons for the highest simulated pump power. As expected in a planar microcavity, the polariton density peaks at the centre of the dual-DBR cavity and is uniform along the y-axis. The simulated polariton population (integrated at the WS position along the y-axis) as well as the energy shift of each UP and LP peak are used as the benchmarks for the nonlinearity calculation in PhC structures. This calculation was repeated for eight pump powers (Figure 4d in the main text).

Figure R17 shows the results for the polariton population under the highest pump power in the PhC structure studied in our simulation. Notably, one can see that, compared to the planar cavity, in this case, the polariton population is inhomogeneously distributed along the PhC y direction. This effective field and population confinement can be more clearly seen in the 1D cuts shown in the right panels. The as-simulated populations (integral population at the WS position along the y-axis) and energy shifts of each UP and LP polariton were thus compared with those from the dual-DBR cavity (Figure 4d in the main text) by tuning the pump power to have similar polariton populations.

Such enhancement is qualitatively similar to the situation encountered in micropillar cavities (Light: Sci. Appl. 12, 220 (2023); Phys. Rev. B 73, 193306 (2006)), where the confinement of the photonic wavefunction induces an effective increase of the exciton phase space filling effect. This numerical comparison shows that, indeed, the field confinement induced by the PhC structure can contribute to an enhancement of polariton-polariton interactions.

Concomitantly, the linewidth decreases from 24.8 to 7.0 meV, which is ascribed to the decreased scattering of excitons with phonons (Nat. Commun. 7, 13279 (2016)).

Subsequently, we extracted the Rabi splitting for each temperature and plotted it in Figure R20. Comment 9:
Could the authors further elaborate on the rationale behind Equations (1–4) in the main text? For example, it is unclear why the 1s-2s terms contributing to the energy shift of 2s excitons depend on N_1s but not on N_2s.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for giving us the possibility to further explain our theoretical model. Equations (1-4) describe the blueshift of the four polariton branches depending on the population of 1s and 2s particles, and on the different light-matter fractions. These equations contain similar terms. The first term describes the “self” Coulomb interaction induced blueshift: the exciton is blueshifted by interacting with the other excitons of the same kind. The second term describes the blueshift induced by the Coulomb interaction between excitons of different kinds, e.g., the blueshift of the 1s exciton due to the interaction with 2s excitons, and therefore this term only depends on N_1s, since the blueshift due to N_2s is already included in the first term. The third term describes the “self” blueshift due to phase-space filling, i.e., quenching of the Rabi splitting due to Pauli blocking. The last term corresponds to the quenching of the Rabi splitting, but this time due to the occupancy of states by the other species of excitons. A more detailed description of how to derive these phenomenological equations can be found in Phys. Rev. B 110, 115304 (2024).
Finally, note that upon taking into account the effect of cross-polarized excitons (to answer comment 13 of the current referee), the equations 1-4 have been further generalized to explicitly separate the contributions of co- and cross-polarized excitons (or exciton-polaritons).
